questions.question: Why does exact (brute-force) similarity search become slow as a document corpus grows?
options: It doesn't — exact search speed is unaffected by corpus size
It compares the query against every single stored vector, so its cost grows roughly linearly (or worse) with the number of stored vectors
Exact search only works for corpora under 100 documents
Exact search requires a special type of GPU that becomes unavailable at scale
questions.explanation: Brute-force search checks every stored vector against the query, so as the number of vectors grows, the amount of work (and time) grows proportionally, becoming impractical for large corpora.

questions.question: What trade-off does Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) search make compared to exact search?
options: ANN search is always slower but more accurate
ANN search pre-organizes vectors to check only a smart subset, trading a small amount of accuracy (occasionally missing the true best match) for a large speed improvement
ANN search guarantees finding the exact best match every time, just like brute-force search
ANN search only works for text data, never for images
questions.explanation: ANN algorithms sacrifice a small, usually acceptable amount of retrieval accuracy in exchange for dramatically faster search at scale, which is essential once a corpus grows beyond a small size.

questions.question: A RAG feature's retrieval latency became unacceptable as the document corpus grew from thousands to millions of chunks. Which question best identifies the standard fix?
options: Should we abandon the RAG approach entirely and rebuild from scratch?
Is our vector database using exact or approximate (ANN) search, and is that configuration appropriate for our current corpus size?
Can we just reduce the number of documents to make search fast again?
Is this definitely an embedding model problem rather than a search algorithm problem?
questions.explanation: Slow retrieval at scale is a well-understood, well-solved problem typically addressed by adopting or properly configuring approximate nearest neighbor search, rather than requiring a fundamental rearchitecture.
